chapters.label: Intro
chapters.text: Happy Wednesday, it's November 25th, the day before Thanksgiving, which means half the country is at an airport and the other half is at a grocery store arguing over the last can of cranberry sauce. Here's what you need to know.

chapters.label: 🌤️ Weather
chapters.text: San Antonio is starting the day cold. It's 38 this morning and feels closer to 31, and there's a freeze warning through Thanksgiving morning, so cover the plants and bring in the pets. It warms to a clear 60 by afternoon, then drops to 49 tonight. No rain at all. Thursday is cloudy and in the 50s, and by Saturday we're up to 72.

chapters.label: 🏆 My Teams
chapters.text: The Spurs are in Portland tonight to face the Trail Blazers, tip-off at nine on ESPN, or on KUNP 16 if you're staying local. San Antonio is 15 and 3 and Portland is 11 and 6, so this is a real road test, not a layup. Pour something warm and settle in. It's going to be a late one.

chapters.label: 🇺🇸 U.S.
chapters.text: The Army blew up nearly five tons of old explosives in Middletown, Iowa this morning, and the town of about 350 people is still standing. The stuff was lead azide, a compound that's very touchy. It had been sitting in storage at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant for about twenty years and had degraded to the point that it could go off on its own from a bump. The plan was delayed several times after residents objected and lawyers got involved, because the worry was a cloud of toxic lead dust. The blast went off at nine, a few pops and a faint plume. Fifteen minutes later the EPA said its four monitors had detected zero lead in the air, and the readings held two hours on. The Army called it a huge success, and Middletown's mayor said he felt relieved and vindicated. The Army's account is that the blast was aimed into the ground to keep lead from spreading. Nobody wanted that to be exciting, and it wasn't.

chapters.label: 💻 Tech
chapters.text: Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, and the stock market is behaving like it just got its dog back. Nvidia's board had said he wouldn't return, but President Trump pushed for it, and governance experts say that amounts to overriding the board. Huang has apologized to employees and says he's in therapy. Investors didn't wait around for the details. The stock jumped more than thirty percent in a day, adding roughly nine hundred and fifty billion dollars in value. That's the biggest one-day gain any single company has ever posted, and it's in the neighborhood of all of Walmart. The pitch is that Huang is basically the face of the AI boom, and so much of the market is a bet on it. So the man comes out of therapy and gets a Walmart. Most of us get a worksheet.

chapters.label: 💻 Tech
chapters.text: The FCC just approved up to one million new SpaceX satellites. That's about fifty times the number currently in orbit. They're called Starmind, and they're meant to work as data centers in space, packed with AI chips. FCC chairman Brendan Carr called it a bold new frontier, and the timing is a day before Thanksgiving, which is when you announce things you'd prefer people skim. Here's the catch: the approval doesn't prove orbital data centers can actually work, technically or financially. SpaceX has seven years to launch one working satellite, until 2035 for the first hundred thousand, and until 2040 for the whole million. That's a fourteen-year runway. Elon Musk, who's allied with the Trump administration, just got a very patient regulator and a very large sky.

chapters.label: 🇺🇸 U.S.
chapters.text: More tariffs are coming. The Trump administration says it will hit fourteen economies, including China, the European Union, Japan, India, Vietnam and Brazil. The target is what the U.S. calls subsidizing industries so they overproduce. The U.S. Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, says it'll level the playing field for American workers. Brazil's sugar and aircraft are in the crosshairs, and China faces the highest rates. The move relies on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which lets the government go after unfair trade practices. That matters because the Supreme Court earlier ruled that the Liberation Day tariffs were illegal, so this is the legally tidier route. Most of these new duties aren't expected to kick in until next year. Economists keep warning that tariffs can push up prices for shoppers if businesses pass on the cost, and that's the part you'll feel at the checkout.

chapters.label: 🏛️ Politics
chapters.text: The Army wants to restart helicopter training flights near Reagan National Airport, as early as December first, according to NTSB chair Jennifer Homendy. This is the same airspace where an Army helicopter collided with an American Airlines jet in January 2025, killing sixty-seven people. A yearlong NTSB review found years of ignored warnings about helicopter traffic there. The FAA suspended training flights in May 2025 after two passenger jets had to abort landings when a Blackhawk got too close. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the Pentagon and told the helicopters to take a taxi or an Uber. Now the FAA says it hasn't received a formal request and that it has to approve any restart. Senator Maria Cantwell called the idea exactly the wrong direction. It's a pretty simple question for the FAA: has anything changed since the last time this went badly?

chapters.label: 🎬 Culture & Entertainment
chapters.text: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade turns one hundred tomorrow, and there will be a hundred inflatables, so the numbers line up. Snoopy is the star. He's been in the parade forty-five times since 1968, as a World War One flying ace, an astronaut and more, and this year he finally shows up as Joe Cool, forty-two feet long, in sunglasses and a red sweater, with Woodstock tucked under his arm. It took the beagle forty-five tries to get cool. Also debuting: Bluey, Hello Kitty and a wizard version of Mickey Mouse. There are about eleven thousand volunteers and participants, with roughly a hundred handlers on each big balloon. The catch is the forecast for New York, which looks stormy. High winds can lower or ground the balloons, though the parade will go on either way.

chapters.label: ⚡ Quick hits
chapters.text: A few quick ones. Nearly twenty thousand passengers are expected at San Antonio International today, so give yourself extra time. In China, Shanghai party chief Chen Jining is under investigation for suspected discipline violations. He's the fourth Politburo member to fall in this cycle of Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign. Martha Firestone Ford, who owned the Detroit Lions after her husband died in 2014, has died at 101. In Britain, discount chain Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting eleven thousand jobs at risk, though the stores stay open for now. And EA is adding the AI-recreated voice of the late John Motson to its football game, with his family's blessing, starting tomorrow.

chapters.label: Wrapping up
chapters.text: That's your Wednesday. Stay warm tonight, take it easy at the airport, and go Spurs. I'll catch you tomorrow, hopefully with a full plate and a full stomach.
